name: Compassion fade
statement: Feeling and giving are said to fall as victims are added, starting at the second, and the two largest tests of that claim found nothing or the reverse.
meaning: The claim is about a slope, not a contrast. Proportion dominance is about the denominator and the identifiable victim effect is about a name and a face, while compassion fade says the curve turns down as soon as a second person is added and keeps falling. Slovic drew it as a value function that peaks at one life and declines from there, and called the decline psychic numbing after Robert J. Lifton's term for what let rescue workers function after Hiroshima. Two mechanisms compete. The affect account says the feeling system cannot scale, so eight children move a donor less than one does. Cameron and Payne's motivated account says groups do stir feeling and people shut it down in advance when they expect the bill. The distinction matters because only the second predicts that the fade should vanish when nobody is going to ask for money.

origin.who: Daniel Västfjäll, Paul Slovic, Marcus Mayorga and Ellen Peters
origin.note: Their paper carries the name and the one-versus-two data. The finding itself was in print seven years earlier as a figure: Slovic's 2007 essay shows mean affect and mean donations for Rokia, Moussa and the pair, credited to Västfjäll, Peters and Slovic, in preparation, with no numbers attached and the comment that perhaps the blurring of individuals begins at two. Markowitz and colleagues cite the same work in 2013 as a Decision Research white paper titled "Compassion fatigue: Donations and affect are greatest for a single child in need".

evidence: Västfjäll and colleagues ran four studies, three of them on Swedish undergraduates. Study 1a, on 208 people, gave hypothetical donations of 37.7 SEK in the single-child conditions against 26.3 SEK for two children, t(205) = 5.88, p < .001, with affect ratings of 3.7 against 3.3, t(205) = 2.87, p < .01. Study 1b put real money on it. Its 168 participants could give their earnings to Save the Children for Rokia (n = 47), for Moussa (n = 51), or for both (n = 70), and gave 24.5 SEK to one child against 21.5 SEK to two, t(166) = 1.67, p < .05, with affect at 3.5 against 3.0, t(166) = 2.81, p < .01. Study 2, on 107 people, measured facial muscle activity while donations fell across one, two and eight children, 24.9, 23.4 and 21.3 SEK, linear trend F(1,103) = 12.01, p < .001. Zygomaticus activity, which tracks positive affect, ran .41, .12 and .09 across the same conditions, F(1,103) = 8.90, p < .001. Cameron and Payne supplied the mechanism study. Their Experiment 1 showed 120 students one or eight children from Darfur and told half that a donation question was coming. Compassion showed no main effect of help request, F(1, 116) = 1.15, p = .29, none of victim number, F(1, 116) = 0.34, p = .56, and an interaction at F(1, 116) = 4.61, p = .03, partial eta squared .04. Markowitz, Slovic, Västfjäll and Hodges carried the pattern to animals. Their Study 3 paid 171 students $5 in single dollar bills and asked for a real donation to panda conservation. Non-environmentalists gave $3.50 for one panda, $2.83 for two and $2.25 for eight, linear contrast F(1, 82) = 5.29, p = .02, r = -.25, while environmentalists gave $2.50, $3.30 and $2.93 with no linear effect, F(1, 85) = .68, p = .41. Butts, Lunt, Freling and Gabriel pooled 41 studies, 95 independent samples and 13,259 participants, and their abstract reports that victim group size negatively affects helping intent, helping behaviour, anticipated positive affect and perceived impact, but not empathic concern.

replication.headline: The largest direct replication, on 1,177 people using the original materials, found more compassion for eight children than for one.
replication.detail: Hagman, Tinghög, Dickert, Slovic and Västfjäll rebuilt Cameron and Payne's Experiment 1 with 1,177 US participants in a two by two by two design, powered to detect a small effect. The interaction that the original rested on came out at F(1, 1,173) = 0.012, p = 0.913, partial eta squared 0.000, against the original's partial eta squared .04. The main effect of victim number ran the wrong way: compassion was higher for the eight children than for the one, F(1, 1,173) = 23.549, p = 0.000, partial eta squared 0.020, in both the help-request and no-help-request conditions. Mood fell further after eight children, F(1, 1,173) = 15.473, p = 0.000, partial eta squared 0.013. Donation amount showed no interaction, F(1, 1,173) = 0.099, p = 0.754. The manipulation itself did not hold: 53.4% of the help-request group and 59.2% of the no-help-request group said they had thought about donating while rating their feelings. Splitting the whole sample by whether people expected to be asked, which should have been the friendliest possible test, still produced no interaction. Hart, Lane and Chinn had already run two large tests of the individual-versus-group contrast. Their Study 1, on 924 MTurk participants, found no difference across four appeal types on feelings, F(3, 916) = 1.45, p = .23, or donation amount, F(3, 916) = .95, p = .41. Study 2, on 1,085 Qualtrics panellists, likewise found nothing on feelings, F(1, 1079) = .053, p = .82, or donation amount, F(1, 1079) = .002, p = .96. Against those sit Markowitz's three studies, whose whole-sample linear trend across one, two and eight pandas reached F(1, 165) = 4.93, p = .03, and the Butts meta-analysis, whose abstract reports the effect in the predicted direction across 95 samples. The disagreement is the finding.

study.cite: Hagman, W., Tinghög, G., Dickert, S., Slovic, P., & Västfjäll, D. (2022). Motivated down-regulation of emotion and compassion collapse revisited. Frontiers in Psychology, 13, 801150.

limits: The drop from one victim to two, which is the claim that makes compassion fade more than a restatement of scope insensitivity, rests on a thin base. In the only one-versus-two study with real money, Västfjäll's Study 1b, the gap was 3 SEK on a t of 1.67 with 98 people in the single conditions and 70 in the two-child condition. The larger and cleaner-looking gap, 37.7 against 26.3 SEK, came from the hypothetical study. Every study in the original paper except one was run on undergraduates at a single Swedish university, and Markowitz's three were run on students at one American university. Sample sizes at the origin are small where the effect is claimed to be a slope: Markowitz's Study 3 split 171 participants across three donation conditions and two self-identified groups. The Butts meta-analysis is the only pooled estimate this entry located, and its correlations, confidence intervals and publication-bias tests could not be read, because the full text is paywalled and no accepted manuscript was found through Crossref, Unpaywall, OpenAlex or Semantic Scholar; the direction reported above comes from the abstract alone. A field study, Meier's analysis of real-world online donations in Nonprofit and Voluntary Sector Quarterly, returned 403 on every attempt and its results are not reported here. A preregistered replication of Västfjäll's Experiments 1a and 3 is listed on ResearchGate under the title "Revisiting Singularity and Compassion Fade", dated 2025; no fetchable copy was found on OSF, Crossref, Europe PMC or the authors' pages, so nothing from it appears on this page.
misreadings: Cameron and Payne are cited as having demonstrated compassion collapse, and their Experiment 1 did not. When help was requested, compassion toward one victim was only numerically higher than toward eight, F(1, 59) = 1.18, p = .28. The significant simple effect was the other one: with no help requested, eight victims drew more compassion than one, F(1, 57) = 3.87, p = .05, partial eta squared .06. Their result is a reversal in the no-request condition, not a fade in the request condition. Second, compassion fade is not compassion fatigue. The clinical term describes the erosion of a carer's capacity over time; this is a cross-sectional response to how many people are in one appeal, and the original Decision Research white paper used the wrong one of the two names. Third, the effect is not the identifiable victim effect renamed. That effect contrasts a named person with statistics, this one holds identifiability fixed and counts heads, and the two can be dissociated: Hart, Lane and Chinn crossed appeal type with imagery on 1,085 people and moved neither. Nor is it the singularity effect. Kogut and Ritov put that name on the gap between one identified victim and a group, and it is covered under the identifiable victim effect. Majumder and colleagues keep the two apart, treating compassion fade as the version that makes victim number a continuous measure. Fourth, the curve that appears in talks and textbooks, peaking at one life and declining, is a drawing. Slovic's Figure 11 is a model with an unlabelled vertical axis, published alongside a study then in preparation, and nobody has measured the function it depicts. Fifth, a reader who takes the effect as settled should note that its own proponents do not. Hagman and colleagues, four of whom work on this literature and one of whom wrote the 2014 paper, published the failure themselves.
